scope: Re-evaluation of the MIT and Stanford entries in the previously documented eight-offering, seven-university pool. This is not a census of all courses worldwide, nor full-course reading.

selection.Stanford: Retain selected core. The reviewed lecture gives rigorous finite-dimensional definitions, coordinate uniqueness, norm axioms and Gram-Schmidt including dependent input. Its real-vector convention needs explicit translation for complex problems.
selection.MIT: Retain selected core. The three short notes provide the strongest signed-component and 3D geometry bridge. They require independently written proof expansions, boundary conditions and advanced exercises; they are not by themselves a comprehensive vectors chapter.

documents.title: Dot Product
documents.reading_method: Official PDF text supplied by the web reader; complete body and attribution page read. Direct local download failed with TLS/read timeouts; no local hash or visual diagram audit is claimed.
documents.content_used: Coordinate dot product; law-of-cosines connection to geometry; real orthogonality test and squared norm. Nonzero qualifications for angle and zero-vector cases must be supplied.

documents.title: Components and Projection
documents.reading_method: Official PDF text supplied by the web reader; complete body and attribution page read. Direct local download failed with TLS/read timeouts; no local hash or visual diagram audit is claimed.
documents.content_used: Signed scalar component onto a unit direction and normalization of a nonunit direction. Independently distinguish that scalar from the projection vector; negative components are valid, whereas lengths are nonnegative.

documents.title: Cross Product
documents.reading_method: Official PDF text supplied by the web reader; complete body and attribution page read. Direct local download failed with TLS/read timeouts; no local hash or visual diagram audit is claimed.
documents.content_used: Coordinate definition, sign and order, distributivity and nonassociativity, area and right-hand orientation. The source explicitly identifies the vector-entry determinant as a mnemonic and omits the Lagrange-identity proof; the chapter must independently supply the proof.

documents.title: Lecture 3: Linear algebra review
documents.reading_method: Complete official PDF body read through overlapping web text ranges; local PDF text cross-checked. Page 30 additionally rendered and visually inspected to verify the negative-right-angle anomaly.
documents.content_used: Finite-dimensional vector spaces, span, independence, basis uniqueness, coordinate extraction, real Euclidean norm, RMS, inner product, Cauchy-Schwarz and unsigned angle. General rank/inverse/similarity content was read as context and is not a reason to expand this chapter without bounds.

documents.title: Lecture 4: Orthonormal sets of vectors and QR factorization
documents.reading_method: Complete official PDF body read through overlapping web text ranges; local PDF text cross-checked. Page 16 additionally rendered and visually inspected to verify the zero-residual skip branch.
documents.content_used: Orthonormality, rectangular versus square orthogonal matrices, preserved geometry, coefficients, prefix-span Gram-Schmidt invariant, dependent-input skip branch, orthogonal complements and unique decomposition. Detailed QR factorization is later-chapter context.

reconciliation.source: Stanford Review PDF page 30 (slide 3-30), contrasted with page 29
reconciliation.finding: Page 29 defines an unsigned arccos angle; page 30 also lists -pi/2 for orthogonality.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: For nonzero real vectors define theta in [0,pi]; orthogonality gives theta=pi/2. The zero vector is algebraically orthogonal to every vector but has no direction or angle.

reconciliation.finding: The word component denotes a signed scalar, not a vector.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: For b nonzero, signed component is (x dot b)/norm(b); projection vector is ((x dot b)/(b dot b))b; projection length is abs(x dot b)/norm(b). If b is unit, the formulas simplify but the scalar/vector distinction remains. Reversing b changes the signed component, not the projection onto span(b).

reconciliation.finding: Basic Gram-Schmidt assumes independent input. Generalized Gram-Schmidt explicitly skips a zero residual instead of normalizing it.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Maintain span of accepted vectors equal to the span of processed inputs. Normalize only a nonzero residual. A zero residual means the current vector lies in the previous span, including a zero first input. In finite precision, exact zero and a chosen numerical tolerance are different decisions.

reconciliation.source: Stanford Review PDF pages 26-31 and Stanford QR PDF pages 2-7
reconciliation.finding: These selected Stanford pages treat real vectors and transpose, not complex Hermitian geometry.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Use x* y for the chapter's complex convention, conjugate-linear in the first slot. Euclidean norm is sqrt(sum abs(x_i)^2). Orthogonal projection onto span(b) is b(b* x)/(b* b). Do not use x^T x as a complex squared norm; x=(1,i) has x^T x=0 and x* x=2. This complex extension is independently derived and reconciled with Oxford, not falsely attributed to these real-only pages.

reconciliation.finding: The selected pages do not define general induced matrix norms. Stanford Review page 26 gives the Euclidean vector norm and its axioms.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: If a question uses ||A||_2, explicitly define the induced/operator norm sup_{x!=0} ||Ax||_2/||x||_2, rather than silently confusing it with Frobenius norm. Supply an independent proof or a separately reviewed written source for any advanced operator-norm result. Do not credit a matrix-norm theory to these selected notes.

reconciliation.finding: The source's dimension-infinity parenthesis says no basis, in a finite-dimensional review context.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Keep this chapter finite-dimensional, or say no finite basis when discussing infinite dimension. The zero space has the empty basis and dimension zero. Do not claim that every infinite-dimensional space lacks a basis.

recommended_question_checks: Test projection direction reversal and nonunit rescaling using a concrete vector pair; distinguish invariant projection from sign-changing scalar component.

For weighted inner product x*G y, change both numerator and denominator. Example G=diag(4,1), x=(2,0), b=(1,1): projection is (8/5,8/5), residual=(2/5,-8/5), and b*G residual=0. Euclidean projection (1,1) is not the weighted projection.
Show a Gram-Schmidt trace with a zero or dependent middle input followed by a genuinely new direction. Do not halt the whole procedure or divide by zero.
Distinguish U*U=I for an orthonormal column family from UU*=I, which additionally requires a square complete basis. For a proper subspace UU* is its projector.
For Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle equality, separate arbitrary complex dependence from nonnegative real alignment. For triangle equality of nonzero vectors, dependence alone is insufficient.

Validate 3D cross-product sign by dotting the result with both operands and checking squared magnitude through the Lagrange identity; the right-hand rule is meaningful only when the cross product is nonzero.
